summary: Background: Mental health and well-being services generate substantial operational and client-level data. Review-level evidence on how data-driven methods support service delivery remains fragmented across technologies and settings. Objective: This study aimed to synthesize review-level evidence on data-driven methods relevant to mental health and well-being service delivery, including business intelligence (BI), data visualization, and machine learning (ML), and identify applications, implementation challenges, and evidence gaps. Methods: We conducted an umbrella review following Joanna Briggs Institute methodology and the PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) 2020. The original searches of Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, ACM Digital Library, and PsycINFO were completed on January 27, 2026. During revision, supplementary PubMed and Embase searches were conducted on September 22, 2026. For both supplementary databases, the search was restricted at the database-search stage to publications from 2021 to the current date and to review/systematic review records; eligibility screening then retained the original January 27, 2026, evidence cutoff. All records were independently screened by 2 reviewers using Covidence (Veritas Health Innovation); the reviewer pair differed between the original and supplementary search phases. Eight structured reviews were critically appraised using the JBI checklist and synthesized narratively. Results: Eight structured reviews were included (3 systematic reviews, 4 scoping reviews, and 1 umbrella review). Seven reviews contributed primary study or source-level evidence, while one umbrella review synthesized 44 reviews. The retrieved evidence was dominated by AI and ML, including conversational agents, natural language processing, and clinical decision support, whereas dedicated BI and operational data visualization syntheses were sparse. Two reviews directly addressed mental health service delivery, 4 were adjacent or partially direct, and 2 were indirect but relevant. Only one review focused specifically on mental health helplines. Service-level benefits were reported more consistently than sustained clinical benefits, although the evidence remained heterogeneous and partly indirect. Safety and implementation concerns included symptom worsening, bias, hallucination, privacy, trust, integration barriers, and inequitable access. Conclusions: Review-level evidence relevant to mental health and well-being services is uneven and concentrated on AI/ML. Because the search required all 3 concept blocks, BI- and visualization-focused reviews may have been under-retrieved. BI and operational data visualization, helpline-specific implementation, long-term effectiveness, safety, and equity require more direct and prospective evaluation before findings can be generalized across service settings. Trial Registration: OSF Registries 10.17605/OSF.IO/8NQBC;
title: Data-Driven Methods Supporting Mental Health and Well-Being Service Delivery: Umbrella Review

summary: Background: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) flares are common and unpredictable. Current monitoring relies on episodic clinical visits and laboratory testing, thereby limiting the ability to anticipate disease worsening. Wearable devices may support continuous remote monitoring, but models must account for missing real-world data, heterogeneous consumer devices, and the distinction between symptomatic disease activity and systemic inflammation. Objective: The study aimed to develop and evaluate deep learning (DL) time-series models using wearable-derived physiological data to predict symptomatic and inflammatory RA flares up to 28 days in advance. Methods: In a prospective cohort study, adults with RA used a smartwatch (Apple Watch; Apple Inc), a wearable fitness tracker (Fitbit; Google LLC), or a smart ring (Oura Ring; Oura Health Oy). Daily wearable-derived heart rate, heart rate variability, and step-count were harmonized across devices and linked with smartphone-based patient-reported outcomes (PROs) and available C-reactive protein results. Symptomatic flares were defined using longitudinal RAPID3 (Routine Assessment of Patient Index Data 3) scores, and inflammatory flares were defined using a prespecified C-reactive protein threshold. Classical machine learning and DL models were trained to predict daily flare vs remission status at 0-, 7-, 14-, 21-, and 28-day horizons. Model evaluation used a temporally ordered 70/30 within-participant train-test split. Performance was assessed using receiver operating characteristic area under the curve (ROCAUC), area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC), and participant-level sensitivity. This prediction-model analysis was not prospectively registered. Results: Forty-nine participants contributed 5624 days of overlapping wearable and clinical data. Participants used Apple Watch (n=31), Fitbit (n=15), or Oura Ring (n=3). DL models outperformed machine learning models using imputed wearable data, with average ROCAUC improvements of 5.3% for symptomatic flares and 18.4% for inflammatory flares, and AUPRC improvements of 9.3% and 44.1%, respectively. For 7-day-ahead prediction, transformer models incorporating wearable-derived physiology and demographic features achieved ROCAUCs of 0.95 for both symptomatic and inflammatory flares, with AUPRCs of 0.92 and 0.91, respectively. Adding daily PRO improved participant-level sensitivity for inflammatory flare prediction from 0.67 to 0.87. Performance remained stable across prediction horizons for up to 4 weeks. Conclusions: Wearable-derived physiological signals analyzed with DL may support personalized forecasting of symptomatic and inflammatory RA flare states weeks in advance. By integrating passive digital biomarkers with PROs, this approach offers a scalable framework for proactive RA monitoring that could help identify disease exacerbations earlier than episodic clinical assessment alone. Further validation in larger, more diverse cohorts and prospective studies is needed to determine whether wearable-guided forecasting improves clinical decision-making, timely intervention, and long-term outcomes.
title: Predicting Rheumatoid Arthritis Flares Using Wearable Device Data: Deep Learning Study

summary: Background: Substance use disorders account for a significant portion of the disease burden attributed to mental health globally, but measurement remains suboptimal. Substance use measurement is over-reliant on retrospective recall, often over long periods of time. However, the episodic, contextual, and event- or time-contingent nature of substance use calls into question the validity of these traditional retrospective measurement methods. One method to overcome these limitations is ecological momentary assessment (EMA), which repeatedly samples participant behaviors and experiences in real time, in the context in which they occur. Objective: This review aimed to systematically identify studies using EMA to measure substance use, provide a comprehensive overview of the EMA methods used, and develop a checklist for improving the reporting of methodological information for future EMA studies in this field. Methods: Studies published between 2018 and 2026 were sourced from PubMed, MEDLINE, Scopus, and PsycINFO via Ovid databases on March 31, 2026, using terms related to EMA, digital phenotyping, passive sensing, daily diary, and specific terms for each drug type. Studies that actively or passively assessed thoughts and/or behavior in the participants’ natural environment/daily lives, in a repeated manner, at or close to the behavior of interest (substance use), using either automatic prompts or notifications, were included. Studies were not excluded according to populations, age, setting, or study design. This study was preregistered on the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO; CRD42023400418). Results: The search identified 12,487 articles, of which 1236 were reviewed in full; 581 studies were included and extracted, resulting in 431 (n=126,733 participants) unique datasets. Most studies were conducted in the United States (348/431, 80.7%) and focused on alcohol (364/431, 84.5%) and cannabis use (172/431, 39.9%) with or without the presence of other substance use. Alcohol and cannabis measurement co-occurred the most in 128 of 431 (29.7%) unique datasets. Phencyclidine, bath salts, cough syrup, crack, depressants, prescription sedatives, prescription tranquilizers, steroids, khat, buprenorphine, gamma-hydroxybutyrate, kava, and kratom were only measured in one dataset each. This review found limited reporting consistency across compliance, completion windows, attrition rates, survey duration, and data collection technologies in EMA substance use studies. Conclusions: This review provides the first comprehensive cross-substance synthesis of EMA methodologies used to measure substance use. In contrast to previous reviews focused on individual substances or narrower methodological issues, it compares methodological characteristics across substance groups and identifies common design and reporting gaps. The findings provide practical recommendations to improve the transparency, comparability, reproducibility, feasibility, and data quality of future EMA studies. Greater consistency in reporting missing data, compliance, survey duration, and prompt completion windows, alongside further integration of wearable technologies and research on underexplored substances, will be important for strengthening the real-world application of EMA in substance use research.
title: Measuring Substance Use With Ecological Momentary Assessment: Scoping Review of Methods and Key Recommendations for a Methodological and Reporting Framework

summary: Background: Large language models (LLMs) have shown promise in generating virtual patients for health care applications. However, whether LLM-generated virtual patients can reproduce patient-reported priority rankings remains uncertain. Objective: We evaluated whether LLM-generated virtual hypertension patients could approximate real patient-reported perspectives, and whether retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) improved alignment with patient-reported priority rankings. Methods: A total of 20 patients from multiple regions completed structured questionnaires ranking priorities across 7 domains related to AI-assisted hypertension management. A total of 8 LLMs were evaluated under 3 simulation conditions: unconstrained generation, patient-specific simulation, and RAG-enhanced simulation. For unconstrained generation, each model produced 20 virtual patient profiles, each constructed by grouping baseline variables into the study categories and selecting the most frequent category across 10 repeated generations. For patient-specific baseline and RAG-enhanced simulations, each model generated 10 complete questionnaire responses per participant and condition; the modal complete 4-item ranking within each domain was selected as the final ranking. Model-generated rankings were compared with patient-reported rankings using total accuracy, top-1 accuracy, and full accuracy. In addition, 5 hypertension clinicians independently inferred patient-priority rankings while blinded to both real patient responses and LLM outputs, providing a human reference benchmark. Results: Aggregated unconstrained virtual patient profiles varied across models, with 45%‐55% having college-level education, and 75%‐95% using antihypertensive medication. In patient-specific baseline simulations, total accuracy ranged from 46.3% to 71.4%. RAG improved all 3 accuracy metrics across the eight models, increasing mean total accuracy from 62.8% to 76.6%, top-1 accuracy from 51.6% to 72.9%, and full accuracy from 22.2% to 49.4% (all <.001). The largest mean domain-level gains occurred in safety escalation awareness and emotional support and reassurance. Qwen-RAG achieved the highest total accuracy (86.1%) and full accuracy (64.3%). In descriptive comparisons, its corresponding values exceeded those of the clinician consensus (72.5% and 45.0%), while top-1 accuracy was numerically similar (80.7% vs 80.0%). Conclusions: LLM-generated virtual hypertension patients can moderately approximate real patient perspectives, but unconstrained aggregated profiles differed demographically, behaviorally, and clinically from the enrolled reference cohort under the study conditions. RAG substantially improves concordance between virtual patient rankings and patient-reported priorities and may provide a scalable methodological approach for incorporating patient-perspective proxies into digital health research contexts. Trial Registration: Chinese Clinical Trial Registry ChiCTR2500102798; https://tinyurl.com/2vahxsed
title: Evaluating Large Language Model–Generated Virtual Hypertension Patients as Proxies for Real Patient Perspectives: Comparative Study

summary: AI-driven clinical decision support systems can prepare executable orders, communicate with patients, and initiate multistep workflows, raising unresolved questions about delegated clinical authority. This viewpoint proposes a 5-level clinical autonomy gradient: informational support (A0), advisory decision support (A1), human-confirmed execution (A2), bounded delegated action (A3), and adaptive autonomous management (A4). Classification applies to a task-action pair within its deployment workflow. Execution authority and case-specific human authorization anchor assignment; decision influence, temporal reach, and scope adaptability describe the configuration. The action-enablement boundary (A1-A2) introduces executable action preparation requiring explicit, informed, case-specific authorization before release. The delegation boundary (A2-A3) permits execution without contemporaneous, case-specific authorization. We adapt an automation scope of practice to record permissions and operating conditions, and an autonomy safety case to link authority to deployment-specific evidence and residual risks. Proposed controls address effective human review, interacting systems, proportionate governance, and withholding, downgrading, or suspending actions when supporting conditions fail. Applications to documented systems and hypothetical scenarios illustrate classification reasoning without establishing reliability or delegated-action safety. Greater autonomy is optional; A1 or A2 may remain appropriate. Independent evaluation must assess classification agreement, feasibility, implementation burden, and effects on care.
title: From Decision Support to Delegated Clinical Action: Governing the Autonomy Gradient of AI-Driven Clinical Decision Support Systems

summary: Background: Emergency departments (EDs) depend on rapid, reliable triage for patient safety and flow. The Manchester Triage System (MTS) is widely implemented but exhibits known interrater variability. Large language models (LLMs) have emerged as potential decision-support tools for triage and early assessment, yet real-world comparative evaluations remain scarce. Objective: This study aimed to compare clinician and LLM performance on ED triage accuracy, specialty assignment, diagnostic recommendations, and admission prediction in a real-world cohort. Methods: In a retrospective cohort study, 305 walk-in ED encounters at a German tertiary-care hospital were analyzed. A nurse performed real-time MTS-assessment and initial specialty assignment at presentation. Each anonymized case was independently evaluated by 4 physicians and 12 LLMs from 4 providers (OpenAI, Google, Anthropic, and Mistral). Triage agreement was assessed against 2 reference standards: a consensus human label (ground-truth 1 [GT1]) and real-time nurse-assigned MTS-triage (ground-truth 2 [GT2]). For human raters, a leave-one-out variant of GT1 (LOO-GT1) assessed incorporation bias. The primary statistic was quadratic-weighted Cohen κ (unweighted κ reported alongside). Secondary outcomes were directional triage errors (over- or undertriage, |Δ|≤1), specialty top-1 accuracy, per-case precision, recall, -score of recommended diagnostics, and admission prediction (sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value [PPV], and negative predictive value [NPV]). Results: Median age was 45 (IQR 31‐62) years; 188 (61.6%) patients were male; admission rate was 20.1% (56/278). Against GT1, human-rater (physicians and nurse) accuracy ranged 0.59‐0.83 (quadratic-weighted κ 0.60‐0.88; unweighted κ 0.35‐0.74), and LLM accuracy 0.35‐0.70 (quadratic-weighted κ 0.46‐0.72; unweighted κ 0.11‐0.53). Under LOO-GT1, human-rater weighted κ fell to 0.48‐0.81. Only 1 clinician (Doctor 1, weighted κ 0.81) retained agreement clearly above any LLM, while 3 LLMs (Gemini-3.5-flash=0.72, GPT-5.5=0.69, and GPT-5=0.66) exceeded the LOO-corrected agreement of the remaining 4 human raters. One-off agreement exceeded 86% for all raters and models. Vs GT1, overtriage ranged 6%‐56% and undertriage 6%‐36%. Vs GT2, corresponding ranges were 11%‐62% and 5%‐30%. Against the study specialty reference, physician specialty-assignment accuracy ranged 0.88‐0.93 and LLM accuracy 0.62‐0.80. Against the operational triage-pathway specialty assignment, the corresponding ranges were 0.81‐0.82 and 0.57‐0.75. Model diagnostic recommendation -scores ranged 0.55‐0.69. Admission prediction demonstrated high sensitivity (0.73‐0.95) and NPV (0.90‐0.96), but modest PPV (0.25‐0.41). Conclusions: In a real-world ED cohort, 1 clinician (Doctor 1, a specialist physician) had the highest urgency agreement point estimate under both GT1 and LOO-GT1. Under LOO-GT1, 3 contemporary LLMs reached agreement that exceeded that of the other 4 clinicians. For specialty assignment, all clinicians remained clearly ahead of the best LLM. LLMs showed strong sensitivity and high NPV for admission prediction, but modest PPV precludes autonomous use. Because both reference standards are empirical rather than outcome-anchored gold standards, findings represent agreement against expert consensus and routine practice rather than an absolute correctness benchmark, and support a complementary, human-in-the-loop role for LLM-based decision-support in ED triage and early assessment.
title: Evaluating Human and AI-Based Triage Performance in the Emergency Department: Real-World Cohort Study

summary: Background: Problematic social media use (PSMU) is linked to depression, anxiety, and loneliness, requiring valid measurement tools. The Bergen Social Media Addiction Scale (BSMAS) is the most widely used PSMU measure internationally, but has not been validated in Czech adults. Objective: This study aimed to (1) validate the Czech BSMAS by evaluating structural validity, internal consistency, measurement invariance, and construct validity, and comparing latent-factor and network representations; and (2) evaluate, in a multivariable prediction-modeling framework with an independent replication sample, whether item-level BSMAS scores predict depression, anxiety, and loneliness better than the conventional sum score. Methods: Two independent nonprobability convenience samples of Czech adults were recruited online via snowball sampling (primary: N=3297; replication: N=514). Structural validity was assessed with confirmatory factor analysis; internal consistency with α and ω. Measurement invariance across gender (configural, metric, and scalar) and differential item functioning across age were assessed. Construct validity was explored through Spearman correlations with depression, anxiety, and loneliness (total, emotional, and social). Latent and network models were compared using the Bayesian information criterion (BIC). For prediction, 5 algorithms compared the BSMAS sum score with the 6 individual items as predictors, using repeated 10-fold cross-validation; performance was quantified with out-of-sample and root-mean-square error. The item-level comparison was additionally evaluated with models fixed in the primary sample and applied unchanged to the replication sample, and with sociodemographic characteristics held constant (registered on Open Science Framework: v9emk). Results: A one-factor model fit well (=101.5, <.001; comparative fit index [CFI]=0.993; root-mean-square error of approximation [RMSEA]=0.056) and reproduced in the replication sample. Internal consistency was high (α=0.87; =0.87). Scalar invariance across gender was supported; 2 of 6 items showed differential item functioning across age. Correlations were moderate with depression (ρ=0.31‐0.38) and anxiety (ρ=0.32‐0.45), small with emotional loneliness (ρ=0.28‐0.29), and negligible to small with social loneliness (ρ=0.03‐0.16). The latent model was more parsimonious than the network model (ΔBIC=–59.32). Item-level representation modestly outperformed the sum score for depression (²=0.15 vs 0.10) and anxiety (²=0.16 vs 0.11). This advantage was reproduced in the replication sample, held with models fixed in the primary sample (Δ²=0.069, 90% CI 0.040‐0.100, and 0.067, 90% CI 0.043‐0.093) and after sociodemographic adjustment, and was not accounted for by weighting items by their standardized factor loadings. More flexible algorithms did not outperform linear regression. Loneliness, especially its social dimension, was poorly predicted by BSMAS scores. Conclusions: In these samples, the Czech BSMAS showed a predominantly unidimensional structure and high internal consistency, with scalar invariance across gender but age-related differential item functioning in 2 items. Item-level scoring offered a small, reproducible predictive advantage for depression and anxiety, although absolute predictive performance was low. Replication in representative samples is needed before population-level or clinical application.
title: Psychometric Properties and Predictive Performance of the Czech Bergen Social Media Addiction Scale for Mental Health Outcomes: Validation and Multivariable Modeling Study in an Adult Convenience Sample

summary: Background: During the COVID-19 pandemic, older adults living in geriatric care facilities were especially limited in their social interactions because of their vulnerability. Care homes often preferred broad isolation measures to avoid the risk of infection among residents. Digital contact tracing systems (DCTS) developed during the COVID-19 pandemic have the potential to overcome the practice of general isolation in geriatric care facilities, but a prerequisite for their successful implementation is acceptance among nursing staff. Objective: This study aimed to investigate nursing staff’s acceptance of such wearable devices for use within geriatric care facilities and the conditions the technology must meet to increase the likelihood of nursing staff’s acceptance, based on a scenario-based prototype for a digital, wearable-based contact tracing system. Methods: The study used a sequential mixed methods design. Initially, an exploratory literature review provided the foundation for conceptualizing the prototype for the contact tracing system. In the next step, focus groups were conducted among nursing staff with and without prior experience with digital contact tracing at work. Building on those results, a survey study on the prototype’s acceptance was conducted among nursing staff in Germany. The focus group interviews, as well as the survey study, were based on the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT). Results: Based on the few studies that focused on nursing staff’s acceptance of digital contact tracing in medical occupations and the results of the focus group interviews, the scenario-based prototype was developed as a wearable with varying characteristics for nursing staff and residents of geriatric care facilities. The prototype was evaluated as generally favorable by the nursing staff participating in the survey study (n=329), specifically under high-threat pandemic preparedness conditions. Furthermore, the survey study indicates that nursing staff’s intention to use the wearable-based contact tracing system was significantly associated with performance expectancy (β=0.291; <.001), as well as choice of wearable (β=0.174; <.001), and usefulness under threatening conditions (β=0.251; <.001). Extending the UTAUT model by context-specific predictors explained 51.6% (=0.516; = 50.973; <.001; Bonferroni-Holm [BH] corrected =.001×6=.006) of the variance in the intention to use DCTS in geriatric care facilities. This marks a significant increase of explained variance of 7% (=0.074; Δ=16.699; <.001) in comparison to the standard UTAUT model (²=0.446; = 66.954; <.001; BH-corrected =<.001). Conclusions: Nursing staff perceived the proposed scenario-based prototype of a DCTS to be especially useful when no other protective measures, such as vaccines or tests, are available, which is a highly probable scenario. Therefore, preparedness strategies should consider digital contact tracing as one potential component of future pandemic preparedness. Trial Registration: OSF Registries osf.io/82TVA; https://osf.io/82tva
title: Development and Acceptance Evaluation of a Scenario-Based Prototype of a Digital Contact Tracing System in Geriatric Care Facilities: Results From an Exploratory Literature Review, Focus Groups, and a Survey Study
